extracted.intended_audience: lawyers, legal scholars, policymakers, and students studying administrative law, sanctions, and terrorist-designation procedures
extracted.subtask_description: Legal and procedural standards governing designation of Foreign Terrorist Organizations (FTOs) and Specially Designated Global Terrorists (SDGTs) under AEDPA, IEEPA, Executive Order 13,224, and OFAC regulations, including avenues for challenge and consequences of designation.

rubrics_metrics.name: FTO designation criteria (AEDPA)
rubrics_metrics.description: Under AEDPA, the Secretary of State may designate a group as an FTO if the group (1) is foreign; (2) engages in “terrorism” or “terrorist activity,” or has the intent to engage in terrorist activity; and (3) threatens the security of the United States or its citizens.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statutory definitions: “terrorism” defined per 22 U.S.C. § 2656f(d)(2) as “premeditated, politically motivated violence perpetrated against noncombatant targets by subnational groups or clandestine agents;” “terrorist activity” defined in 8 U.S.C. § 1182(a)(3)(B)(iii) (hijacking, threats to compel action, use of biological/chemical weapons, etc.). The D.C. Circuit treats the question whether a group threatens national security as a political question, limiting judicial review to the first two elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: AEDPA procedural requirements for designation
rubrics_metrics.description: Before designating an FTO the Secretary of State must report her intention to the Speaker and Minority Leader of the House, the Senate President pro tempore, Majority and Minority Leaders of the Senate, and members of certain congressional committees via a classified statement; within seven days of notifying Congress she must publish the designation in the Federal Register and create an administrative record of the reasons supporting the designation (which may include classified and unclassified information).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The classified statement may include hearsay and uncorroborated statements; the government need not disclose classified information to the FTO but must disclose it to a court on judicial review. Once the Secretary notifies Congress, OFAC may (but is not required to) freeze the group's assets.

rubrics_metrics.name: FTO revocation / delisting procedure (AEDPA)
rubrics_metrics.description: A designated FTO may petition the Secretary of State for revocation by showing circumstances have changed sufficiently that designation is no longer warranted; an FTO may file a revocation petition every two years; the Secretary must decide whether to revoke within 180 days of receipt; if no petition is filed within five years, the Secretary must review the designation herself; revocation may also occur by Act of Congress or by the Secretary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Revocation decisions are subject to the same procedural requirements as designations, including publication in the Federal Register.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial review standard for FTO designations
rubrics_metrics.description: On review in the D.C. Circuit, courts examine only the administrative record created during the designation process plus any classified information submitted by the government and may invalidate a designation or denial of revocation if the Secretary’s decision was “arbitrary, capricious, an abuse of discretion, or otherwise not in accordance with law,” “contrary to [a] constitutional right,” “in excess of statutory jurisdiction, authority, or limitation,” or “lacking substantial support in the administrative record.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because courts generally defer to agency heads when statutory procedures are followed, the Secretary of State’s decisions are given substantial deference if procedural requirements are met. The D.C. Circuit has limited review regarding the 'threat' element as a nonjusticiable political question.

rubrics_metrics.name: IEEPA declaration and reporting requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: IEEPA permits the President to declare a national emergency in response to “any unusual and extraordinary threat, which has its source in whole or substantial part outside the United States, to the national security, foreign policy, or economy of the United States,” and requires the President to report statutory findings to Congress explaining the circumstances necessitating the emergency, why they constitute an unusual and extraordinary threat, the specific actions intended, why those actions are necessary, and which foreign nations or entities will be affected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: After declaring an emergency the President must report changes in the situation to Congress at least once every six months. National emergencies expire on their anniversary unless renewed. Presidents frequently implement IEEPA authorities through executive orders.

rubrics_metrics.name: IEEPA regulatory/blocking authority (including pendency-of-investigation freeze)
rubrics_metrics.description: Under IEEPA, during a declared national emergency the President may issue regulations to investigate, regulate, or prohibit certain monetary, credit, or securities transactions involving foreign entities and may nullify or void transactions involving property in which designated foreign countries or nationals have an interest; amendments permit the President to block an entity’s assets “during the pendency of an investigation.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regulations under IEEPA apply to all property within U.S. jurisdiction or its financial institutions. IEEPA allows classified information to be provided to courts on review but does not provide an explicit standard for judicial review beyond APA standards; it does not itself create a cause of action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Executive Order 13,224 authority for SDGT designations
rubrics_metrics.description: Executive Order 13,224 authorizes the Secretary of State, after consultation with the Secretary of the Treasury and the Attorney General, to designate foreign persons who have committed or pose 'a significant risk of committing' terrorist acts against the United States as SDGTs; it authorizes the Secretary of the Treasury to block property of persons owned or controlled by, or acting for or on behalf of, those listed in the Annex or designated by the Department of State.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EO 13,224 was issued pursuant to IEEPA's emergency; once designated as an SDGT an entity cannot access property or money located within the United States or its financial institutions. The EO vests substantial discretion in the Treasury Secretary and allows blocking during investigations.

rubrics_metrics.name: OFAC delegation, blocking powers, and license authority
rubrics_metrics.description: The Secretary of the Treasury delegated the power to designate SDGTs and to block assets to the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC); OFAC can freeze (block) assets of designated entities and may block assets during the pendency of an investigation; the Secretary of the Treasury/OFAC may also grant licenses for certain specified transactions (e.g., payment of lawyers’ fees).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OFAC executes blocking orders, publishes names of entities with assets blocked pending investigation, and can issue both general and specific licenses under 31 C.F.R. § 501.801 and related provisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: OFAC regulatory procedures and limits on remedies
rubrics_metrics.description: OFAC’s internal regulations (31 C.F.R. §§ 594.101–.901; 501.101–.901) provide limited guidance for entities seeking to challenge OFAC actions: only two provisions (§§ 501.806–.807) describe how an entity may attempt to change its status as an SDGT (e.g., request a meeting with OFAC’s director), and those options are constrained; OFAC’s director has complete discretion whether to grant or deny meetings and may hear evidence but is not required to do so; regulations do not provide a way for entities with assets blocked pending investigation to challenge the blocking order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In practice OFAC thus exercises near-complete control over the fate of an SDGT after designation, and affected entities frequently face limited administrative avenues for relief.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope difference: Department of State vs OFAC designation powers
rubrics_metrics.description: Under AEDPA the Department of State may designate only foreign groups meeting statutory requirements (including threat to U.S. security); under EO 13,224 and OFAC’s authority, the Treasury can designate persons (including domestic entities) that are owned/controlled by, assist, sponsor, or are otherwise associated with terrorist groups, permitting designation of entities that do not directly threaten the country.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because OFAC can target entities based on support/association, it can designate nonprofits and other groups without intent to harm the U.S. The Treasury (OFAC) also controls asset-blocking and has broader discretionary authority than State in practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consequences of designation and collateral effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Designations can result in blocking/freezing of assets, restriction of transactions, criminal sanctions for third parties providing material support, deportation risk for alien group members, and civil penalties for financial institutions that fail to report or comply.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Specially Designated Terrorist Muhammad Salah could not access money without OFAC license limited to 'basic maintenance,' could not travel or maintain bank accounts, and lived under these constraints since 1995 without a statement of reasons—facts invoked to argue First and Fifth Amendment violations. OFAC’s blocking orders can be imposed pending investigation, intensifying immediate harm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of classified information in the administrative record
rubrics_metrics.description: The administrative record supporting a designation may include both classified and unclassified information; the government need not disclose classified information to the designated entity but must disclose it to a court on judicial review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because classified evidence may be relied upon (and hearsay is permitted in some submissions), designated entities may lack access to the full evidentiary basis for their designation, complicating ability to rebut and increasing deference afforded to agency decisions when procedures are followed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reporting, renewal, and expiration formalities for national emergencies
rubrics_metrics.description: When invoking IEEPA authorities, statutory findings must be reported to Congress; national emergencies must be renewed annually (they terminate on their anniversary unless continued), and the President must report changes in the situation at least every six months. The Secretary of the Treasury was delegated reporting requirements for the emergency created by EO 13,224.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These formalities provide statutory checkpoints (reports, semiannual updates, renewals) but in practice Presidents have extended EO 13,224 annually since issuance.
